vjimc-1996-cat1-01.title: Area as a function of the point, AM-GM
vjimc-1996-cat1-01.body:
Let $a,b>0$. The triangle exists only if the tangent meets both axes away from the origin, i.e. $x_0z_0\ne0$. By symmetry in both axes it suffices to take $x_0>0$, $z_0>0$; the other quadrants give the mirror images.

The tangent at $T$ is
$$\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{zz_0}{b^2}=1 ,$$
which meets the axes at $P=\left[\frac{a^2}{x_0},0\right]$ and $Q=\left[0,\frac{b^2}{z_0}\right]$. The triangle $OPQ$ has area
$$S=\frac12\cdot\frac{a^2}{x_0}\cdot\frac{b^2}{z_0}=\frac{a^2b^2}{2x_0z_0}.$$
So we must maximise $x_0z_0$ on the ellipse. By AM-GM,
$$\frac{x_0}{a}\cdot\frac{z_0}{b}\le\frac12\left(\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}+\frac{z_0^2}{b^2}\right)=\frac12,$$
with equality iff $\frac{x_0}{a}=\frac{z_0}{b}$, i.e. $\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}=\frac{z_0^2}{b^2}=\frac12$. Hence $x_0z_0\le\frac{ab}2$ and
$$S\ge\frac{a^2b^2}{ab}=ab,$$
with equality exactly at $x_0=\frac a{\sqrt2}$, $z_0=\frac b{\sqrt2}$.

**Answer:** the points $T=\left[\pm\frac a{\sqrt2},\pm\frac b{\sqrt2}\right]$ (all four sign choices), with minimal area $ab$. ∎

vjimc-1996-cat1-01.title: Calculus in one variable (official approach)
vjimc-1996-cat1-01.body:
In the first quadrant write $x_0=\frac ab\sqrt{b^2-z_0^2}$ with $0<z_0<b$. As above, $S=\frac{a^2b^2}{2x_0z_0}$, so
$$S(z_0)=\frac{ab^3}{2z_0\sqrt{b^2-z_0^2}} .$$
$S$ is smallest where $\psi(z_0)=z_0^2(b^2-z_0^2)$ is largest. We have $\psi'(z_0)=2z_0b^2-4z_0^3=2z_0(b^2-2z_0^2)$. This is positive for $z_0<\frac b{\sqrt2}$ and negative for $z_0>\frac b{\sqrt2}$, so $\psi$ has its maximum $\frac{b^4}4$ at $z_0=\frac b{\sqrt2}$. As $z_0\to0^+$ or $z_0\to b^-$, $S\to\infty$ (the triangle degenerates).

Then $x_0=\frac ab\sqrt{b^2-\frac{b^2}2}=\frac a{\sqrt2}$, and $S_{\min}=\frac{ab^3}{2\cdot b^2/2}=ab$. Reflecting in the axes gives the other three points $\left[\pm\frac a{\sqrt2},\pm\frac b{\sqrt2}\right]$. ∎

vjimc-1996-cat1-02.title: Check a small case
vjimc-1996-cat1-02.body:
From the recurrence, $a_2=2a_1-2a_0=2-2=0$. But for $n=2$ the sum is
$$\sum_{k=0}^{1}\binom{2}{2k}=\binom20+\binom22=2\ne0 .$$
So the formula is false.

**Answer: No.** ∎

vjimc-1996-cat1-02.title: Compare closed forms (official approach)
vjimc-1996-cat1-02.body:
For $n\ge1$, $\sum_k\binom n{2k}$ is the number of even-size subsets of an $n$-element set, which is $2^{n-1}$ (from $(1+1)^n+(1-1)^n=2\sum_k\binom n{2k}$). It equals $1$ for $n=0$.

The recurrence $a_{n+2}=2a_{n+1}-2a_n$ has characteristic equation $t^2-2t+2=0$ with roots $1\pm i$. Fitting $a_0=a_1=1$ gives
$$a_n=\tfrac12(1+i)^n+\tfrac12(1-i)^n=2^{n/2}\cos\frac{n\pi}4 .$$
This is $0$ for $n=2$ (and in fact for all $n\equiv2\pmod4$), whereas $2^{n-1}>0$. So the two sequences differ.

**Answer: No.** ∎

vjimc-1996-cat1-03.title: Bound the variables one at a time
vjimc-1996-cat1-03.body:
Let $\varphi(t)=\frac{t}{1+t^2}$. For $t\ge1$, $\varphi'(t)=\frac{1-t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}\le0$, so $\varphi$ is decreasing on $[1,\infty)$, and $\varphi(t)>0$ for $t>0$.

The equation is symmetric, so it suffices to show it has finitely many solutions with $x\le y\le z$; every solution is a permutation of one of these. Then $\varphi(x)\ge\varphi(y)\ge\varphi(z)$.

**$x$ is bounded.** $\frac1{1996}=\varphi(x)+\varphi(y)+\varphi(z)\le3\varphi(x)$, so $\frac{3x}{1+x^2}\ge\frac1{1996}$, i.e. $x^2-5988x+1\le0$. This forces $x\le5988$, so $x$ takes finitely many values.

**For fixed $x$, $y$ is bounded.** Put $r_x=\frac1{1996}-\varphi(x)$. Since $\varphi(y),\varphi(z)>0$, a solution needs $r_x>0$. Then $r_x=\varphi(y)+\varphi(z)\le2\varphi(y)$, i.e. $\frac{2y}{1+y^2}\ge r_x$, so $r_xy^2-2y+r_x\le0$. This bounds $y$ ($y\le 2/r_x$). So for each of the finitely many $x$ there are finitely many $y$.

**For fixed $x,y$, $z$ is determined up to two choices.** We need $\varphi(z)=s:=r_x-\varphi(y)$, i.e. $sz^2-z+s=0$ with $s>0$. A quadratic equation has at most two roots.

So there are finitely many triples with $x\le y\le z$, hence finitely many solutions altogether. (Possibly none; "finitely many" includes zero.) ∎
